summary:
Bingöl is a province in eastern Turkey with no documented provincial divergence from the national legal position on trans people. No province-specific ordinance, separate legal system or distinct enforcement pattern has been recorded for Bingöl, so a trans visitor here stands under the framework that applies across Turkey.

That framework is hostile by design. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 on a leaked omnibus draft, the '11th Judicial Package', which would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour it defines as 'contrary to biological sex and general morality'. Participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony would carry penalties of up to four years' imprisonment. The draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and require permanent infertility as a condition, and would punish health professionals who provide such care. Human Rights Watch described it as one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft. The measure had not been passed as of that reporting, but its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, presented at its launch by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, found that anti-LGBTI+ hostility in Turkey has been institutionalised as explicit state policy: senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, while regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. Kaos GL recorded 313 violations in 2025, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, including 299 detention decisions.
tangentialFactors:
Street-level enforcement elsewhere in Turkey indicates what document checks can involve. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in that reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One woman detained stated that police issued no fines but documented her anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied. Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints are required to produce original identity documents, creating a direct outing risk where appearance does not match a passport gender marker. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender individuals disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Prison conditions bear directly on any prolonged stay. Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex in gendered facilities; a trans man was held in a women's prison, confirmed when the case of the transgender prisoner Poyraz, found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025. Coordinated demands for an independent investigation came from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın, with accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reporting that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Prison Insider's country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, no staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, a binary and heteronormative administration, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints processes that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening nationally. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued, risking the profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
localsOnly:
For resident LGBTI+ people in Bingöl, the same national framework governs daily life, and the province offers no separate legal shelter from it. Kaos GL's reporting records that hate speech from senior officials and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner have shaped the conduct of state bodies, including regulatory and supervisory authorities that restrict expression and artistic freedom. This is a matter of domestic civic space: the environment documented is one in which violations are encouraged from above rather than arising as residual prejudice.

The 2008 Human Rights Watch report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the depth of the regime rather than as a statement of current law.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bingöl-specific enforcement data, provincial police practice, hate-crime incidents or local care access arrangements were found in the source material. Whether the GBT-style stop pattern documented in Istanbul is applied to trans visitors in Bingöl is unresolved and not sourced here.

The status of the '11th Judicial Package' as of the time of writing is unresolved in these sources: Human Rights Watch reported it as a leaked draft in October 2025, opposed by 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association, and it had not been passed at that point. Provisions described are proposals, not current law.

Whether Bingöl's own health facilities apply the Kayseri-style medical-board reporting circular, and whether any provincial hospital declines transition-related care, is not sourced. The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 is described at national level only.
